CausalChain: SF3B2 upregulation -> altered splicing of DNA repair regulators (RAD51, BRCA1) -> compromised DNA repair -> increased susceptibility to viral DNA integration (facilitated by chronic viral infection) -> genomic instability -> enhanced metastasis -> poor liver neoplasm prognosis
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that the upregulation of SF3B2, together with other spliceosome components such as SF3B1 and EIF4A3, contributes to liver neoplasm progression by inducing aberrant alternative splicing of pivotal DNA repair regulators like RAD51 and BRCA1. This mis-splicing leads to diminished DNA repair efficiency, creating an environment of genomic vulnerability. In cases of chronic viral infection, such as with hepatitis B virus, this compromised repair capacity predisposes cells to viral DNA integration, further exacerbating genomic instability. The cumulative effect of these disruptions is an increased propensity for metastatic dissemination and worsened clinical outcomes. To test this hypothesis, we will employ state-of-the-art transcriptomic analyses including long-read and single-cell RNA sequencing, along with CRISPR-based perturbation assays, to quantitatively link SF3B2 expression with splicing alterations, DNA repair defects, and instances of viral integration in liver cancer models.
Abstract: We propose that the upregulation of splicing factors, notably SF3B2, in concert with key regulators such as SF3B1 and EIF4A3, drives liver neoplasm progression by perturbing the alternative splicing of DNA repair genes including RAD51 and BRCA1. This mis-splicing diminishes the cellular capacity for DNA damage repair, fostering genomic instability, and—particularly in a background of chronic viral infection (e.g., hepatitis B)—may increase the likelihood of viral DNA integration. Leveraging advanced transcriptomic profiling (e.g., long-read and single-cell RNA sequencing) and CRISPR-based functional genomic screens, our hypothesis aims to delineate the contribution of splicing dysregulation to the cascade of genomic instability, metastatic spread, and poor clinical outcomes in liver cancer. This integrative framework refines the speculative original mechanism by embedding it within a broader splicing regulatory network and utilizing state-of-the-art technology for comprehensive mechanistic insight.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis posited that SF3B2 upregulation leads to altered splicing of DNA repair regulators, thereby facilitating viral DNA integration and promoting liver cancer progression. Our revised hypothesis retains the core causal chain but expands it by incorporating other spliceosome factors (SF3B1, EIF4A3) known to influence tumor aggressiveness, thereby addressing recent evidence. We have nuanced the step involving viral DNA integration by emphasizing its facilitation in the context of chronic viral infections, supported by advanced genomic detection techniques. Finally, we enhanced practical implementability by proposing the use of cutting-edge transcriptomic and CRISPR methodologies to validate each step of the causal chain, ensuring that the refined concept remains novel, coherent, and experimentally testable.
